chapter.title: The fire spreads: France falls, Britain holds

cards.body: On 10 May 1940, the day Winston Churchill became Britain's prime minister, German tanks rolled into a forest the French thought no tank army could get through quickly. France had built a thick fire wall on the side of its house facing the flames, and **the fire came in by the side door**. Britain's house stood across 20 miles of water, and fire can't walk across water: it has to throw sparks through the air.
cards.simpler: On 10 May 1940, the same day Winston Churchill became Britain's prime minister, German tanks rolled into a forest. The French thought no tank army could get through it quickly. Picture France as a house that built a thick fire wall on the side facing the flames. But **the fire came in by the side door**. Britain's house stood across 20 miles of water. Fire can't walk across water. It has to throw sparks through the air.

cards.prompt: France's army is about as big as Germany's, and France and Britain together have more tanks. Germany still wins in six weeks. What's your best guess?

options.text: Germany secretly had twice as many soldiers
Germany hit where France wasn't looking, and moved faster than France could react
The French soldiers just didn't want to fight

whyNot.a: That's the numbers story, not the 1940 one: the armies were about the same size, so size can't explain six weeks.
whyNot.c: That blames the people, not the plan: the side-door picture is about where the fire got in, not who was standing inside.

cards.reteach: Go back to the fire wall. France put its strongest defence right where it expected the fire, and Germany didn't go there. A big army in the wrong place, moving slowly, loses to a smaller push in the right place, moving fast.

cards.title: The side door
cards.body:
France's fire wall was the *Maginot Line*, a chain of concrete forts along its border with Germany. In a way it worked: the main German attack went around it, through the *Ardennes*, a hilly forest in Belgium and Luxembourg that French planners thought was too slow going for a big tank army.

Then came speed. Tanks raced ahead, *dive-bombers* (planes that drop their bombs in a steep dive) cleared the road, and soldiers on foot caught up later. French commanders reacted in days. German tanks moved in hours.

**France didn't lose because it was smaller. It lost because it was slower.**
cards.simpler: France's fire wall was the Maginot Line, a row of concrete forts on its German border. The main German attack went around it, through the Ardennes. That's a hilly forest in Belgium and Luxembourg that French planners thought was too slow for tanks. Then came speed. Tanks raced ahead, dive-bombers cleared the road, and foot soldiers followed. French commanders reacted in days. German tanks moved in hours. **France didn't lose because it was smaller. It lost because it was slower.**

cards.title: Ten days to the sea
cards.body: On 13 May 1940 German tanks crossed the river Meuse at Sedan, a French town at the edge of the Ardennes. Seven days later they reached the Channel coast near Abbeville. Meanwhile France's best armies and the British had marched north into Belgium to meet the attack they expected, so that one dash cut them off from the rest of France. Paris fell on 14 June, and France signed an *armistice*, a ceasefire on Germany's terms, on 22 June. **The armies were the right size. They were in the wrong place.**
cards.simpler: On 13 May 1940 German tanks crossed the river Meuse at Sedan, at the edge of the Ardennes. Seven days later they reached the coast near Abbeville. France's best armies and the British had gone north into Belgium, expecting the attack there. That one dash cut them off from the rest of France. Paris fell on 14 June, and France signed a ceasefire on Germany's terms on 22 June. **The armies were the right size. They were in the wrong place.**

cards.prompt: A friend says: "France just needed more soldiers in 1940." Which reply fits what actually happened?

options.text: More soldiers in the wrong place wouldn't help. France needed to react fast where the tanks came through.
France should have sent even more of its army into Belgium
Fair enough, the bigger army always wins

whyNot.b: That's exactly what France did, so it can't be the fix: marching north into Belgium is what left the side door open.
whyNot.c: That's the numbers story, not the 1940 one: France was about Germany's size and still lost in six weeks.

cards.reteach: Picture two fire crews of the same size. One parks at the front door and waits, and the other rushes in through the side. What decided 1940 was where the attack came in and how fast each side could react, not how many people were standing around.

cards.title: Why Britain didn't follow
cards.body:
Britain had a gap the fire couldn't walk across: the English Channel, about 20 miles wide at its narrowest. Invading meant carrying soldiers over in slow river barges, and the Royal Navy, far bigger than Germany's navy, was waiting to sink them.

So Germany needed control of the sky first, with planes that could keep British warships away. You'd think the sea was the whole defence. **It was half. The other half was in the air.**

Through the summer of 1940, in what's called the *Battle of Britain*, RAF fighter pilots took on the German bombers again and again. Radar stations on the coast warned them when raids were coming. In September Hitler put the invasion off. It never came.
cards.simpler: Britain had a gap fire can't cross: the English Channel, about 20 miles at its narrowest. Invading meant slow river barges, and the far bigger Royal Navy waited to sink them. So Germany needed the sky first. **The sea was half the defence. The other half was in the air.** Through summer 1940, in the Battle of Britain, RAF fighters took on German bombers, warned by coastal radar. In September Hitler put off the invasion. It never came.

cards.body: Sam finishes a Dunkirk film and tells a friend that's where Britain beat Germany. In fact Dunkirk, from 26 May to 4 June 1940, was an escape from a battle already lost: the Navy hoped to rescue about 45,000 men and, with help from fishing boats and pleasure boats, brought home about 338,000. They left most of their tanks and guns behind, and Churchill told Parliament that wars are not won by evacuations. To spot this mix-up, ask: **did this event win ground, or just survival?**
cards.simpler: Sam finishes a Dunkirk film and tells a friend that's where Britain beat Germany. Not quite. Dunkirk, from 26 May to 4 June 1940, was an escape from a battle already lost. The Navy hoped to save about 45,000 men. With fishing and pleasure boats helping, it brought home about 338,000, leaving most tanks and guns behind. Churchill told Parliament wars are not won by evacuations. So ask: **did this event win ground, or just survival?**

cards.prompt: France fell in six weeks. Britain never fell. Which line explains both?

options.text: France's army was small, so it lost. Britain's army was big enough to hold.
Germany beat France with speed through a gap France thought was safe. It couldn't cross to Britain without winning the air, and it didn't win it.
Dunkirk pushed the Germans back, so they never reached Britain

whyNot.a: That's the numbers story, not the 1940 one: France's army was about as big as Germany's and still lost in six weeks.
whyNot.c: That's the escape, not the reason: Dunkirk saved soldiers from a lost battle. It didn't push anyone back.

cards.reteach: Two houses, two different problems. France's fire got in through the side door and spread before anyone could react. Britain's fire had to jump 20 miles of water, which meant winning the sky first, and in the Battle of Britain the RAF made sure Germany couldn't.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
France fell in six weeks because Germany attacked fast through the Ardennes, the one place France thought was safe, and cut off its best armies in Belgium. Britain held because Germany had to win the sky before crossing 20 miles of sea guarded by the Royal Navy, and **in the Battle of Britain it couldn't**.

Tomorrow: why Hitler, stuck at the Channel, turned east and picked a far bigger fight.
cards.simpler: France fell in six weeks. Germany attacked fast through the Ardennes, the one place France thought was safe, and cut off its best armies in Belgium. Britain held because Germany had to win the sky before crossing 20 miles of sea guarded by the Royal Navy, and **in the Battle of Britain it couldn't**. Tomorrow: why Hitler, stuck at the Channel, turned east and picked a far bigger fight.

cards.body: Open any map app and find Dover and Calais to see how narrow that gap is. Then find Sedan, at the edge of the Ardennes, and trace a line west to Abbeville on the coast. That's the six weeks in one swipe.
cards.simpler: Open any map app and find Dover and Calais. See how narrow that gap of sea really is. Then find Sedan, at the edge of the Ardennes, and trace a line west to Abbeville on the coast. **That's the six weeks in one swipe.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain how France, with an army as big as Germany's, lost in six weeks, and why Britain, alone across 20 miles of water, did not.
